questions.q: Inside the `log` function, what does `shift` accomplish right after `local level="$1"`?
options: It capitalizes the remaining arguments
It removes $1 from the argument list, so $* now refers to everything after the level
It converts $* into an array
It deletes the function's local variables
questions.explain: `shift` drops the first positional argument, so after it runs, $1 (and $*) refer to what used to be $2 onward -- in this case, the full log message.

options: local makes the variable run faster
Without local, assigning region inside the function would overwrite a variable of the same name in the caller's scope
local is required syntax for all function bodies
local converts the variable to a constant
questions.explain: Bash function variables are global unless declared local. Skipping local risks silently clobbering a same-named variable elsewhere in the script.

questions.q: A function needs to hand back a computed string value, like a release tag, to its caller. What's the correct mechanism?
options: return "the-string"
echo the value, then capture it in the caller with $(...)
Set a global variable named RETURN
exit with the string as the exit code
questions.explain: return in bash can only pass back a numeric exit code (0-255), never a string. To hand back actual data, a function echoes it and the caller captures it with command substitution.

questions.q: `is_release_dir_valid` ends with `[[ -d "$dir" && -f "$dir/app.conf" ]]` and has no `return` statement. What does calling code see?
options: A syntax error, because every function needs an explicit return
The function's exit code is simply the exit code of that last [[ ]] test
The function always returns 0 regardless of the test
Nothing -- the function produces no usable result at all
questions.explain: When a function has no explicit return, its exit code is the exit code of the last command it ran -- here, the [[ ]] test, making it usable directly in an if condition.

questions.q: Why does Northbridge's script compute `SCRIPT_DIR` with `$(cd "$(dirname "${BASH_SOURCE[0]}")" && pwd)` before sourcing `lib/common.sh`?
options: To make the script run faster
So the source path is resolved relative to the script's own location, regardless of the directory the script is called from
It's required by bash syntax to use source at all
To disable set -euo pipefail temporarily
questions.explain: Resolving the script's own directory first means `source "${SCRIPT_DIR}/lib/common.sh"` works correctly no matter what directory the user was in when they ran the script.
